title: Flat generic closures recover equivariance after a domination
statement:
Let $k$ be a field, let $S_0$ and $S$ be integral finite-type $k$-schemes, and let $u:S\to S_0$ be a birational morphism. Let $t:T\to S_0$ be H-projective, with $T$ integral of finite type over $k$ and generic fibre $N$ a smooth geometrically integral curve. Write $K=k(S_0)=k(S)$. Let $D\subset N$ be a finite etale closed $K$-subscheme, possibly empty, and let $L\subset T$ be its schematic closure. Let a finite group $H$ act compatibly on $k,S,S_0,T,u,t$ and preserve $D$. Suppose $v:V\to S_0$ is a birational morphism of integral finite-type $k$-schemes and $r:S\to V$ satisfies $vr=u$. Let $T_V\subset T\times_{S_0}V$ and $L_V\subset T_V$ be the schematic closures of $N$ and $D$. Assume $T_V\to V$ is H-projective, flat and finitely presented with geometric fibres pure of dimension one, and $L_V\to V$ is finite, flat and finitely presented. No action on $V$ or $r$ is part of the data. Put $P=T_V\times_VS$ and $M=L_V\times_VS$, as closed subschemes of $W=T\times_{S_0}S$. Then $P$ is integral and $k(P)=k(N)$ via the generic inclusion; $P\to S$ is H-projective, flat and finitely presented with geometric fibres pure of dimension one; and $M\subset P$ is finite, flat and finitely presented over $S$. The generic fibres are canonically $N$ and $D$, with their maps to $T$ and $\operatorname{Spec}K$. Moreover $P$ and $M$ equal the schematic closures of $N$ and $D$ in $W$, so are independent, as closed subschemes of $W$, of the chosen domination $r$ with the above properties. The action on $W$ restricts to actions on $P$ and $M$, making their structural maps to $T$ and $S$ equivariant. The subscheme $M$ is also the schematic closure of $D$ in $P$; in particular $M=\varnothing$ when $D=\varnothing$. Birational means an isomorphism between dense open subschemes. Pure dimension one means that every irreducible component of every geometric fibre has Krull dimension one.

All group actions are by automorphisms, may be nonfaithful, and commute with the displayed maps; they may act on the ground field. H-projective means admitting a closed immersion into a finite-dimensional projective space over the target, independently of the name of the acting group. Normal means that all local rings are integrally closed domains. Schematic closure is the closed subscheme defined by the kernel of restriction of functions to the specified subscheme.

Notions used: [def-weil-field], [def-pc-integral-scheme], [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], [def-kun-projective], [def-sc-function-field], [def-pc-fibre-product], [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], [def-pc-geometrically-irreducible], [def-weil-etale-morphism], [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism], [def-weil-closed-immersion], [def-weil-flat-morphism], [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation], [def-weil-geometric-fibre], [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension].

source.place: Exposé X, Theorem 3.4, proof Step 2, printed p.160: after flattening the proper transforms equal base changes. Kernel-of-restriction and torsion-free argument as in Stacks divisors.tex, lemma-strict-transform-flat (Tag 080F); morphisms.tex, lemma-characterize-scheme-theoretically-dense (Tag 01RE). Equivariance by invariance of the kernels is the agent-written enhancement.

proof.text: Write $\eta=\operatorname{Spec}K$. The birational identifications in the hypotheses give the same generic point and field for $S_0,S,V$. Explicitly, for an affine $\operatorname{Spec}A\subset S_0$ and a nonempty affine $\operatorname{Spec}B\subset V$ over it, dominance makes $A\to B$ injective and birationality identifies $\operatorname{Frac}B=\operatorname{Frac}A=K$. Thus $(A\setminus\{0\})^{-1}B=K$: it contains $K$ and is contained in $K$. The affine generic fibres glue to $\operatorname{Spec}K$. The same applies to $u$; the equation $vr=u$ makes the generic map of $r$ the identity under these identifications. This uses the stated dense-open definition of birationality and the cited affine description of function fields.

Schematic closure retains the prescribed generic closed subscheme. Here is the affine calculation, also fixing all generic identifications. On an affine $\operatorname{Spec}A$ of an integral base with fraction field $K$, put $E=A\setminus\{0\}$, and take an ambient affine $\operatorname{Spec}B$. A closed subscheme of the generic fibre has ideal $J\subset E^{-1}B$; its closure has ideal $I=\ker(B\to E^{-1}B/J)$. Localization is exact, so $E^{-1}I=J$: equivalently, if $b/e\in J$, then $b/1\in J$ and $b\in I$. Consequently $(B/I)\otimes_AK=E^{-1}B/J$. The cited affine kernel description applies because the generic-point map is quasi-compact (its inverse image on an affine is a point), its base changes are quasi-compact by clause (3) of the cited permanence statement, and composing with a closed immersion (an affine morphism) keeps quasi-compactness. Apply this calculation to $N,D$ over $V$, then use Step 1 and fibre-product associativity. It gives $(T_V)_\eta=N$, $(L_V)_\eta=D$, $P_\eta=N$, $M_\eta=D$, with exactly their given maps to $T$ and $\eta$.

source.place: Tag 01R8, lemma-quasi-compact-scheme-theoretic-image; algebra.tex Tag 00CS, proposition-localization-exact; schemes.tex Tag 01I4, lemma-fibre-product-affine-schemes

proof.text: Base change along $r$ preserves flatness and finite presentation, and preserves finiteness for $L_V\to V$. Thus $P\to S$ is flat and finitely presented and $M\to S$ is finite, flat and finitely presented. Base change of the displayed closed inclusions gives $P\hookrightarrow W$ and $M\hookrightarrow P$. The composite $M\hookrightarrow W$ is a closed immersion: on an affine it is the composite of quotient maps $B\twoheadrightarrow B/I\twoheadrightarrow(B/I)/J$, itself a quotient. This verifies closedness rather than inferring factorization from containment of underlying sets.

Choose the finite-projective-space embedding $T_V\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^n_V$ provided by H-projectivity. Its base change is a closed immersion $P\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^n_V\times_VS=\mathbf P^n_S$, by the two cited statements. Its composite with the projective-space projection is $P\to S$. This proves H-projectivity in precisely the finite-dimensional convention of the item, independently of any action on $V$.

source.place: Tag 01WF, lemma-H-projective-base-change, proof via projective-space base change

proof.text: For $s\in S$, put $z=r(s)$. Apply the geometric-purity-to-local-dimension statement to $T_V\to V$: every point of its ordinary fibre at $z$ has local topological dimension one. This application is valid because finite presentation implies local finite presentation. If $\Omega$ is an algebraic closure of $\kappa(s)$, the geometric fibre of $P\to S$ at $s$ is $(T_V)_z\times_{\kappa(z)}\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$. The component-dimension theorem for arbitrary field extension now says that every irreducible component of this scheme has dimension one. Its finite-type hypothesis holds for the fibre of the finitely presented morphism $T_V\to V$. This proves the asserted geometric purity without identifying $\Omega$ with an algebraic closure of $\kappa(z)$.

On every affine $\operatorname{Spec}A\subset S$, $A$ is a domain and $K=\operatorname{Frac}A$. On every affine $\operatorname{Spec}C$ in either $P$ or $M$ mapping into it, the affine flatness criterion makes $C$ a flat $A$-module. The torsion-free-domain lemma and the zero criterion for module localization give an injection $C\hookrightarrow (A\setminus\{0\})^{-1}C$: if $c/1=0$, some nonzero $a\in A$ kills $c$, so $c=0$. The affine fibre-product formula identifies this localization with the coordinate ring of its generic fibre. These affine opens cover both schemes; on their basis the generic restriction of functions is injective. This is the needed schematic generic density, including for the possibly empty $M$.

source.place: Tag 080F, lemma-strict-transform-flat, torsion argument; Tag 01U5, lemma-flat-characterize; algebra.tex Section 00CM, localization

proof.text: We now compute the two actual closure ideals in $W$. Take an affine $U=\operatorname{Spec}B\subset W$ over an affine $\operatorname{Spec}A\subset S$. Its inverse image in $P$ is $\operatorname{Spec}(B/I)$, since $P\hookrightarrow W$ is closed. Step 6 makes $B/I\to(B/I)\otimes_AK$ injective. Hence $\ker(B\to\mathcal O_N(U_\eta))=I$, using Step 2 to identify the generic fibre. Replacing $P,N$ by $M,D$ gives the corresponding equality for the ideal of $M$. The affine kernel description of schematic image therefore identifies $P$ and $M$ with the schematic closures of $N,D$ in $W$. The calculation is on an affine basis, so is an equality of ideal sheaves. A second allowed domination has the same two kernels in the same $W$, proving independence as closed subschemes, not just an abstract isomorphism.

The generic fibre $N$ is integral, hence reduced and irreducible. Its scheme-theoretic image in $W$, which Step 7 identifies with $P$, is the reduced induced closed subscheme on the closure of its topological image, by the reduced-image lemma. The continuous image of a nonempty irreducible space and its closure are nonempty and irreducible: two closed subsets covering the closure would pull back to two closed subsets covering $N$, forcing one to contain its whole image. Thus $P$ is nonempty, reduced and irreducible, hence integral by the cited definition. This does not require all fibres of $P\to S$ to be reduced.

For a nonempty affine $\operatorname{Spec}C\subset P$ over $\operatorname{Spec}A\subset S$, Step 6 gives a nonzero generic affine ring $C_K=(A\setminus\{0\})^{-1}C$, so this generic affine is a nonempty open in $N$. The fraction fields of the domains $C$ and $C_K$ coincide: each is generated by fractions of elements of $C$, and inverting elements of $A$ introduces no new fractions beyond these. Apply the affine-function-field statement to $P$ and $N$. It gives $k(P)=\operatorname{Frac}C=\operatorname{Frac}C_K=k(N)$ via the generic inclusion, with the same maps from $K$ as in Step 2.

For $h\in H$, let $a_h$ be its induced automorphism of $W$. Compatibility on $T,S,S_0$ induces its action on the generic fibre $N$; the hypothesis also preserves $D$ scheme-theoretically. The square of restriction maps on an open $U\subset W$ and $a_h^{-1}U$ commutes: pulling a function back by $a_h$ and then restricting to $N$ is the same as first restricting and pulling back by its generic automorphism. The same holds for $D$. Therefore $a_h^\sharp$ sends each of the two kernel ideals of Step 7 to itself (between these opens); apply $h^{-1}$ for equality. The closed immersions $i_P:P\to W$ and $a_hi_P:P\to W$ have equal ideal sheaves. The equal-ideal-isomorphism lemma gives a unique automorphism $b_h$ with $i_Pb_h=a_hi_P$; likewise obtain $c_h$ on $M$. Uniqueness gives $b_1=1$ and $b_hb_j=b_{hj}$, since their composites with $i_P$ agree; the same applies to $c$. Restriction along $M\hookrightarrow P$ is compatible by this uniqueness. Composing the displayed identities with $W\to T,S$ proves equivariance of both structural maps. The commuting square uses ring isomorphisms only, so also permits nontrivial actions on $k$ and nonfaithful group actions.

source.place: Tag 01QP, lemma-closed-immersion-ideals (2); agent-written restriction-kernel and group-law calculation

proof.text: Finally repeat the kernel computation of Step 7 inside $P$: for an affine $\operatorname{Spec}C\subset P$, the inverse image in $M$ is affine with ring $C/J$, and Step 6 makes $C/J\to(C/J)\otimes_AK$ injective after choosing an affine base chart. Its kernel from $C$ is exactly $J$. Since the generic fibre is $D$, $M$ is the schematic closure of $D$ inside $P$. If $D=\varnothing$, the target of generic restriction is the zero ring on every such affine. Injectivity forces every ring of $M$ to be the zero ring, so $M=\varnothing$. This checks the empty marking without invoking positive degree or a section of the marking.
